fatal_errors: The proposed Y2O3 intervention does not reconstruct the target intervention of varying Mo content in a CoCrFeNiMox-Ni/MoS2-Ag-Cr2O3 composite.
Evidence E2 explicitly reports that Y2O3 had no significant influence on coefficient of friction, contradicting the central claim of consistently reduced friction.
Evidence E1 concerns a different Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 nanohierarchical alloy and does not establish that dilute Y2O3 additions create the same adaptive interface or high-temperature glaze in CoCrFeNi.
The claim of one-to-two orders of magnitude lower wear throughout RT–800 °C is unsupported by the cited evidence.
Critical test parameters—normal load, counterface, speed, sliding distance, and discrete temperatures—are left unspecified, preventing agreement with or direct comparison to the target regime.
explanation: The hypothesis directly addresses the broad wide-temperature tribology problem and proposes a controlled baseline comparison with measurable falsification criteria. However, it is a speculative alternative rather than a reconstruction of the target study. It omits Mo-controlled lattice distortion and sigma-phase formation, the Ni/MoS2-Ag low-temperature lubricant films, and the NiO/silver-molybdate glaze responsible for high-temperature behavior. Its baseline is also inconsistent with the target: the target Mo0.2 composite has its worst wear at intermediate temperature and substantially improved friction and wear at 800 °C, rather than monotonically degrading at high temperature. The experiment is reasonably discriminating but needs the specified 8 N load, Si3N4 counterface, 0.15 m/s speed, 270 m distance, discrete RT/200/400/600/800 °C tests, replication, and direct chemical identification of the proposed glaze. Most importantly, the evidence supports room-temperature strengthening or wear improvement at best and does not validate reduced friction or durable RT–800 °C performance from Y2O3.
